title: The One With Unagi

jokes.text: Remember when I had a monkey? What was I thinking?
jokes.setup: Ross opens with an offhand nostalgic remark about having once owned a pet monkey.
jokes.punchline: His immediate self-questioning ('What was I thinking?') signals absurdity and self-awareness about a genuinely bizarre life choice.
jokes.explanation: Works well as a cold open because it references Ross's actual backstory (Marcel the monkey) without needing explanation. The self-deprecating punchline is quick and character-specific. High character integration because only Ross would have this problem.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I had a monkey! His name was Marcel!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, why are we even talking about this?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't know! It made sense at the time!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, it really didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. It was a terrible idea and I have no idea what I was thinking.

jokes.text: 20 percent is a pretty generous tip. / You know what's more generous? 50 percent!
jokes.setup: Ross defends giving 20% tip as generous.
jokes.punchline: Joey (a waiter) argues that 50% is more generous, completely missing the point that generosity has practical limits — revealing his self-interest.
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Joey's waiter perspective makes this feel specific rather than generic greed humor. The escalating structure ('you know what's even more generous') adds a beat of anticipation that lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: 20% seems high. What about 15%?

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.line: 15%? That's insulting. How about 25%?

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: 25%? For what?

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.line: For listening to you complain about 20%. Now it's 30%.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: You can't just keep raising it!

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.line: I can, and I am. That'll be 40% now.

jokes.text: You know what's even more generous? / I see where you're going.
jokes.setup: Joey begins escalating the tip percentage argument again.
jokes.punchline: Ross cuts him off with 'I see where you're going' — the interruption itself is the joke, as Ross refuses to let the absurd logic continue.
jokes.explanation: The economy here is excellent — the punchline is essentially a non-verbal interruption rendered in dialogue. It caps the tip escalation gag cleanly without overstaying its welcome.

dialogue.line:
Setting up another escalation

Character cuts off the pattern before it gets absurd

jokes.text: Actually, two, because one of them I blackened some teeth. Why'd I do that?
jokes.setup: Joey is lamenting he's down to only three headshots.
jokes.punchline: He then immediately corrects himself — he defaced one by blacking out teeth — and then baffles himself with his own past decision.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character work. The double-beat — the absurd fact (blackened teeth on a professional headshot) PLUS Joey's self-bewilderment at his own action — is very well constructed. Only Joey could deliver this naturally. The 'Why'd I do that?' is the kicker that elevates it beyond a simple joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm almost out of headshots. I need to get new ones made.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What happened to all of them?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I had this one headshot I didn't like, so I drew a mustache on it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, I was bored!

jokes.text: Or, you know, I used to beg for money. It helps if you've got a little of this going on.
jokes.setup: The group discusses ways Joey could earn extra money. Phoebe offers the suggestion of begging.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe demonstrates her 'pitiful beggar face' — a physical expression implying she was actually good at this — played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe — the fact that she has a practiced beggar face, delivered without irony, is perfectly in character with her bohemian past. The visual component (her actually making the face) is what sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: Please, I really need the money. I'm begging you.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown character
dialogue.line: *demonstrates pathetic begging posture with puppy dog eyes*

jokes.text: Wow! I still have it.
jokes.setup: Phoebe demonstrates her pitiful beggar face for the group.
jokes.punchline: She appraises herself with pride — 'I still have it' — treating the ability to look pitifully beggarly as a desirable skill worth maintaining.
jokes.explanation: The two-word punchline 'I still have it' works because it's the exact self-congratulatory phrase you'd use for a talent — applied to something absurd. Economy is nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm very proud of this look. I spent years perfecting it.

jokes.text: I used to get paid for all kinds of medical stuff. Let's see... Well, I don't want to donate sperm again.
jokes.setup: Joey recalls participating in medical experiments for money.
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions he's already donated sperm before — and then, just as casually, rules it out again.
jokes.explanation: Joey casually dismissing sperm donation — a significant personal act — as one item on a mundane to-do list is very Joey. The 'Well, I don't want to...' framing implies he considered it seriously before ruling it out.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm thinking about volunteering for medical experiments. They pay pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That would explain a lot.

jokes.text: I really prefer doing that at the home office.
jokes.setup: Joey says he doesn't want to donate sperm again.
jokes.punchline: He adds 'I really prefer doing that at the home office' — a euphemism that lands as both crude and weirdly corporate at the same time.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of 'home office' (professional, businesslike) with the act being referenced is clever wordplay. Joey's deadpan delivery of corporate language for something primal is perfectly on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not doing it again. Last time they made me go in a room by myself and... let's just say I'm not a fan of the commute.

jokes.text: Joey? What did I tell you about talking while working? / Do it?
jokes.setup: Gunther reprimands Joey for chatting instead of working, as a customer has been waiting.
jokes.punchline: Joey's response — 'Do it?' — reveals he genuinely internalized 'talk while working' as an instruction TO do it, not to stop.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey obtuseness. The one-word question 'Do it?' is a perfectly economical punchline. It simultaneously confirms he was told this before and that he consistently misunderstood. The dramatic irony of Gunther being his boss is also funny.

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: What were you told about talking while you work?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, um, that I shouldn't do it?

dialogue.speaker: Boss
dialogue.line: Right. So why do I keep hearing you talk?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh, I thought you meant I shouldn't talk WHILE I'm working. Like, during. But I can talk before work starts and after work ends, right?

jokes.text: Kicking a guy in the crotch all morning really takes it out of you.
jokes.setup: Rachel and Monica return exhausted from their self-defense class.
jokes.punchline: 'Takes it out of you' — an unintentional (or very intentional) double entendre about groin-kicking being exhausting.
jokes.explanation: A solid pun — the double meaning of 'takes it out of you' vis-à-vis crotch-kicking is funny on its face. Not particularly deep character comedy but the accidental-sounding delivery makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel or Phoebe
dialogue.line: We went to self-defense class today.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel or Phoebe
dialogue.line: By the end, the instructor was exhausted from us practicing on him.

jokes.text: Takes it out of you? [Ross reacts with visible amusement/disbelief at the unintended double meaning]
jokes.setup: Rachel says kicking a guy in the crotch 'really takes it out of you.'
jokes.punchline: Ross's reaction acknowledges the double entendre Rachel apparently didn't notice.
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat extends joke 10 — Ross serving as the audience surrogate who notices what Rachel didn't. Functional but not adding much new comedy beyond acknowledging the previous joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Kicking crotches?

jokes.text: Now we can kick anybody's ass. After one class? I don't think so.
jokes.setup: Monica boasts that after one self-defense class, she and Rachel can kick anyone's ass.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately deflates the claim with common-sense skepticism.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the unagi storyline — Ross being the voice of reason before introducing his own (equally absurd) theory. Standard sitcom straight-man/boaster beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a state of total awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, unagi! It's a freshwater eel!

jokes.text: It's what the Japanese call unagi.
jokes.setup: Ross claims karate expertise and is building to some profound Eastern wisdom.
jokes.punchline: He introduces 'unagi' with great gravitas — which the audience (and Monica/Rachel) immediately suspects is not what he thinks it is.
jokes.explanation: The setup of the episode's A-plot. Ross's pedantic gravitas — 'what the Japanese call...' — when introducing a concept that is (as we immediately learn) a sushi item, is perfectly Ross. His academic self-seriousness is the core comedic engine of this entire subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Unagi is not sushi. Unagi is a freshwater eel. It's very dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, but isn't it served as sushi?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It can be, but that doesn't make it sushi. It's like if I served you a steak on a sushi roll, it wouldn't make it sushi.

jokes.text: Isn't that a kind of sushi? / No, it's a concept. / Yeah, it is. It's freshwater eel.
jokes.setup: Ross introduces 'unagi' as a profound martial arts concept.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately correctly identifies it as sushi; Ross denies it; Monica confirms Rachel — it IS freshwater eel.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's signature moments. The structure is perfect: Ross's pompous setup, Rachel's correct but seemingly naive guess, Ross's dismissal, then Monica's confirmation that Rachel was right. The three-beat structure escalates beautifully. It deflates Ross's academic pretension in a single exchange and sets up the entire episode's comedic thesis — Ross is wrong and he knows everything. Easily scores 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, did you say sushi? I'm so hungry.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, but Ross was just talking about his karate thing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't care about karate. I want spicy tuna roll right now.

jokes.text: Maybe it means that too.
jokes.setup: Monica has just confirmed that 'unagi' literally means freshwater eel in Japanese.
jokes.punchline: Ross refuses to admit defeat, suggesting it might have multiple meanings — a transparently desperate save.
jokes.explanation: Four words of perfect character comedy. 'Maybe it means that too' is Ross refusing to concede while his dignity crumbles — consistent with his character's inability to admit fault. The economy is exceptional; this could have been a full speech but it's delivered as a tiny lifeboat of denial.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Unagi? What is unagi?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a fresh water eel. In Japan, the unagi is considered a delicacy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! I thought you said 'una-gee'. Like, 'una-gee, una-gee, una-gee!'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have no idea!

jokes.text: I would kill for a salmon-skin roll right now.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to hold court on the serious subject of unagi/total awareness.
jokes.punchline: Rachel completely derails the moment by thinking about food — specifically sushi — triggered by their discussion of freshwater eel.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. The word association from 'freshwater eel' to 'salmon-skin roll' is both funny and character-consistent for Rachel (foodie, easily distracted). It also perfectly sabotages Ross's self-important lecture. This line became a fan-quoted moment from this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You always need to be prepared for a surprise attack.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Like this!

jokes.text: Unagi is a state of total awareness. Only by achieving true unagi can you be prepared for any danger that may befall you.
jokes.setup: Ross proceeds with his pompous martial arts lecture despite having just been told 'unagi' means eel.
jokes.punchline: He delivers the definition with absolute straight-faced sincerity and faux-Eastern wisdom, completely ignoring what just happened.
jokes.explanation: Ross's ability to compartmentalize his humiliation and barrel forward with the speech is classic Geller. The faux-mystical language ('may befall you') is funny because it's so overwritten. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The unagi is a freshwater eel. But it's also used to describe a particular style of Japanese cuisine.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's so interesting!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying the eel is also a food preparation method?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Exactly. It's fascinating how one word can have multiple meanings in culinary contexts.

jokes.text: In case someone's trying to steal your bamboo sleeping mat... or your kettle of fish?
jokes.setup: Ross explains that unagi prepares you for 'any danger that may befall you.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's mock-ancient stereotypes ('bamboo sleeping mat,' 'kettle of fish') skewer Ross's appropriated Eastern wisdom as a cliché.
jokes.explanation: Monica's sarcasm here is well-constructed — she's mocking both the concept AND the cultural appropriation implicit in Ross's lecture. The specificity of 'kettle of fish' is particularly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Get her a calendar. That way she can mark the day she met me and... oh wait, that would be every day.

jokes.text: It's one thing being prepared for an attack against each other. Whole other story being prepared for an attack. I don't know.. Surprise! [Ross jumps out and attacks them]
jokes.setup: Ross is lecturing Monica and Rachel about the limits of their self-defense training versus true 'unagi.'
jokes.punchline: He suddenly yells 'SURPRISE!' and physically ambushes them from behind a wall — proving his point with a dramatic (and ridiculous) physical demonstration.
jokes.explanation: The physical escalation is very well earned. Ross goes from pseudo-wise lecture to literally ambushing two women — the contrast between his academic self-seriousness and this chaotic physical act is what makes it land. The build ('it's one thing... whole other story...') is structurally sound.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A spa day? That sounds great! You know what would really get her in the mood? A couples massage.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And then afterwards, you could take her back to the hotel room and... well, let's just say there's a different kind of massage you could give her.

jokes.text: You knew that was coming... but that doesn't mean you have unagi.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel prepared for Ross's attack after he telegraphed it.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately moves the goalposts — their preparedness doesn't count because they 'knew it was coming,' undermining his own demonstration.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Ross moment — he attacks, they're ready, so he immediately discredits their preparedness. It's the comedic logic of someone who can never be proven wrong. Very character-specific and consistent with his insufferable-academic persona.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! I'm both the boyfriend AND the brother here, and I'm very uncomfortable!

jokes.text: If we made reservations, we could have unagi in a half-hour.
jokes.setup: Ross is lecturing seriously about unagi as a spiritual concept.
jokes.punchline: Rachel brings the conversation back to sushi — treating 'unagi' purely as a menu item and cutting through Ross's pseudo-wisdom.
jokes.explanation: The best callback of the episode. 'If we made reservations, we could have unagi in a half-hour' is the perfect button on the unagi-as-sushi running gag. It's a complete, self-contained joke that also works as the ultimate deflation of Ross's pomposity. Earns its 8+ for structure, economy, and quotability — this line is what gets clipped on YouTube.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? Making a gift is way better than buying one. It shows you really care.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's sweet, Joey. What would you make?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, if I were giving my girlfriend a gift, I'd probably just... you know, wrap myself up in a bow.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not a gift, that's just you being creepy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no - see, that's where you're wrong. You put a little fabric softener on first, so it's all soft and nice...

jokes.text: Valentine's Day was two weeks ago, so I wouldn't get her a calendar.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Monica's friends for Valentine's Day gift advice, saying he doesn't know what to get her.
jokes.punchline: Ross's literal-minded and unhelpfully pedantic response — suggesting a calendar is a bad gift because the date has passed — is perfectly dry.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ross pedantry redirected at Chandler. The joke works because it's technically useful advice (don't get a calendar if the holiday passed) while being completely useless in context. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm making a birdhouse out of human hair.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why would you make a birdhouse out of human hair?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, the birds need to know it's a safe place.

jokes.text: And, of course, crotchless panties.
jokes.setup: The gang is offering romantic Valentine's Day gift ideas for Monica.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe adds 'crotchless panties' to the list of romantic ideas with the same casual confidence she'd suggest flowers.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's breezy delivery of an unexpected suggestion lands because of the 'of course' — framing it as obvious. The joke isn't the suggestion itself but the casual confidence with which she makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: A smock-a-lypse.

jokes.text: As appealing as that sounds to her boyfriend... and her brother...
jokes.setup: Phoebe suggests crotchless panties as a gift for Monica.
jokes.punchline: Ross acknowledges his dual role (ex-boyfriend of Rachel, but also Monica's BROTHER) — the second part landing as the actual punchline, implying a deeply uncomfortable level of consideration of Monica's lingerie.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes of the episode. The structure is a perfect double-beat: 'her boyfriend' (expected) then the pause and 'her brother' (unexpected and deeply uncomfortable). Only Ross Geller, Monica's brother, could deliver this. The beat between the two clauses is where the laugh lives. High character integration score is fully justified.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Sock bunnies?! That's not a craft, that's a cry for help!

jokes.text: We promised to make each other gifts this year. / You can't make crotchless panties? / You take scissors and cut..
jokes.setup: Chandler explains they agreed to make each other gifts.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe provides immediately practical DIY instructions for crotchless panties — scissors and cutting — undercutting the romance of handmade gifts.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Phoebe's immediate, helpful practicality — she doesn't see why this is awkward. 'You take scissors and cut..' is funnier for being interrupted, as though the method is so obvious it doesn't need completion. Good extension of the gag.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait a minute... that's my sock!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No it's not.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes it is! I've been looking for that sock for three weeks!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I needed it for the bunny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You made a bunny out of my sock?

jokes.text: I thought so too, until I papier-mached one of my eyes shut.
jokes.setup: Phoebe says making things sounds fun.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals he attempted papier-mâché and accidentally glued his eye shut — an absurdly specific and self-defeating creative failure.
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed. 'Papier-mached one of my eyes shut' is specific, visual, and deeply pathetic in the best sitcom sense. It tells you everything about Chandler's domestic incompetence without overexplaining.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Someone keeps stealing my socks from the dryer!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's not stealing. That's the dryer giving you a gift of mystery and freedom.

jokes.text: I love papier-mache! What did you make? / I made a flar-lar-lar. / What is that? / Nothing!
jokes.setup: Phoebe excitedly asks what Chandler made with papier-mâché.
jokes.punchline: Chandler invents a nonsense word ('flar-lar-lar') to avoid saying what it actually is, then immediately admits it's 'nothing' — implying a failed or embarrassing creation.
jokes.explanation: 'Flar-lar-lar' is a genuinely original comedic invention — a made-up word that sounds like a panicked cover-up. The beat from nonsense word to 'Nothing!' is perfectly timed. The joke works because the audience's imagination fills in what the failed craft project actually was (almost certainly a very bad attempt at something for Monica).

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! I just realized what 'flar-lar-lar' means!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's the sound a baby penguin makes when it's learning to swim backwards in a blizzard!

jokes.text: Have you made anything I can take credit for? / I have, I have! I started making little sock bunnies!
jokes.setup: Chandler desperately asks if anyone has made something he can claim as his own Valentine's gift.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe enthusiastically offers her 'little sock bunnies' — an obviously craft-fair-mom project that is completely wrong as a romantic gift from Chandler to Monica.
jokes.explanation: Decent setup for the sock bunny running gag. The gap between what a romantic Valentine's gift should be and 'little sock bunnies' is the joke. Phoebe's enthusiasm vs. Chandler's desperation is well-matched.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh my God, I forgot to get you a gift! But you know what? That's okay because I got you something even better — I got you... the gift of my presence! Which, let's be honest, is worth like a thousand dollars on the open market.

jokes.text: Oh, for crying out loud! / Wait a minute. That is my sock! / Now it's your little bunny friend.
jokes.setup: Phoebe shows Chandler a sock bunny she is mid-construction.
jokes.punchline: Chandler recognizes it as HIS sock — Phoebe has apparently taken his sock without asking and is converting it into a craft project. 'Now it's your little bunny friend' is her completely unapologetic response.
jokes.explanation: 'Now it's your little bunny friend' is the best line in this exchange — Phoebe's total lack of guilt about sock theft, combined with the condescendingly sweet framing of his property as a 'friend,' is very Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more calm right now? I'm like the poster child for serenity. They should put my picture in the dictionary next to the word 'relaxed.' I'm so chill, I'm practically frozen. In fact, I think I've achieved a state of zen that most monks only dream about!

jokes.text: This actually is a flar-lar-lar. [Chandler shows Monica what he made — a visually awful craft project]
jokes.setup: Earlier Chandler denied knowing what a 'flar-lar-lar' is.
jokes.punchline: He now confirms it's a real (failed) creation — the visual of whatever he actually made being so bad it has no recognizable name.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The reveal that it IS a 'flar-lar-lar' (i.e., a thing so bad it has no real name) works because the word itself sounds like something shapeless and unidentifiable. The visual of the actual object makes this land even harder in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm here for the medical study. I'm Joey Tribbiani.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.line: Welcome, Mr. Tribbiani. What brings you in today?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I understand you're looking for male test subjects, and I'd like to offer my services. I'm very committed to advancing the cause of science.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.line: That's wonderful. The study involves—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But first, how much are you gonna pay me to jerk off?

jokes.text: I just have to go to the place where I made it and pick it up. [Monica clearly bought something at a store rather than making it herself]
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler agreed to make each other Valentine's gifts. Monica asks if Chandler has forgotten.
jokes.punchline: Monica's response — 'I just have to go to the place where I made it and pick it up' — is transparently a store, not a crafting location. She's lying about having made anything.
jokes.explanation: The circumlocution 'go to the place where I made it and pick it up' is brilliantly written — it's technically true of a factory, completely false in spirit, and an exact representation of Monica's control-freak perfectionism refusing to admit a crafting failure.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? But I've been saving up!

jokes.text: I can't believe it! Make the presents! / What? / Just so excited to make the presents!
jokes.setup: Chandler has apparently just realized Monica hasn't made anything either, and Monica realizes he noticed.
jokes.punchline: Monica's overcorrection — screaming enthusiasm about 'making the presents' in an obvious fake-out — is a classic panic move that reveals exactly what she's trying to hide.
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Monica's competitive perfectionism turned inward makes her a terrible liar, and her frantic cover-up is funnier than a smooth one would be. Standard sitcom beats but executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A new study shows that 72% of women find me attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's called 'Joey Tribbiani: A Comprehensive Analysis of Perfection.'

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Joey Tribbiani. With all due respect, I'd like to donate some fluids.
jokes.setup: Joey approaches a medical research receptionist hoping to participate in studies for money.
jokes.punchline: 'With all due respect, I'd like to donate some fluids' — the formal opening phrase applied to this utterly informal and inappropriate request is the gag.
jokes.explanation: 'With all due respect' is a formal business phrase Joey applies to bodily fluid donation — the collision of registers is funny and very Joey. He treats this like a professional pitch meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A study shows that men who are attractive have a better chance of getting ahead in life.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.line: Well, that's not good news for you.

jokes.text: That's too bad. I've been saving up.
jokes.setup: The receptionist tells Joey they're not looking for new research participants.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he's been 'saving up' his bodily fluids — a casually delivered line that implies disturbing levels of preparation for fluid donation.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum impact. 'I've been saving up' is funnier than any longer explanation would be. Joey's casual delivery of something profoundly strange is perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What is wrong with you?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was really weird, Ross.

jokes.text: "Testing the Effects of Joey Tribbiani on Attractive Nurse Receptionist." / Results are back on that one. They're not good.
jokes.setup: Joey scans the schedule of medical studies, finding one he invents on the spot.
jokes.punchline: The receptionist calmly informs him the results of that (fictional) study are already in — and they're not good — a perfect deadpan denial.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. Joey's flirtatious improvised study title is immediately deflated by the receptionist playing along with the fiction JUST ENOUGH to reject him. 'Results are back on that one. They're not good.' is devastating in its calm delivery. The joke works on two levels: it's a rejection AND a commentary on Joey's charm not working.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, technically, it was a very aggressive educational experience. I mean, I learned that my reflexes are slower than I thought, and that Monica's vase was worth more than my dignity.

jokes.text: Danger! Danger! [Ross jumps out at Rachel and Monica in the hallway]
jokes.setup: Ross is on a campaign to prove Monica and Rachel lack 'unagi' by ambushing them.
jokes.punchline: He jumps out from somewhere (presumably a hiding spot) shouting 'Danger! Danger!' — the earnestness of a grown man stalking his friends in the name of karate philosophy.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Ross ambushing people escalates satisfyingly. The sheer commitment of shouting 'DANGER! DANGER!' as a warning/attack hybrid is funny precisely because it's self-defeating — if you warn of danger, you lose the element of surprise you're trying to demonstrate.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? You think you could kick my ass?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Yeah, we could totally kick your ass!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Alright, alright. How about this?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: *makes sudden aggressive move*

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: *screams and jumps back*

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's what I thought.

jokes.text: You're a freak! / Perhaps. / Now I'm curious. At what point during those girlish screams would you have kicked my ass?
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel screamed when Ross ambushed them, proving they were NOT prepared.
jokes.punchline: Ross acknowledges being called a freak ('Perhaps') then smugly points out they screamed like girls instead of fighting back.
jokes.explanation: The 'Perhaps' is the best word — Ross doesn't even contest being a freak, it's beneath his dignity. Then he pivots immediately to the counter-argument. His smug correctness is very Ross. 'Girlish screams' is the needle-scratch punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, it's important to be aware of your surroundings at all times. Awareness is key to—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Surprise!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ow! What the—

jokes.text: Danger! [Ross jumps at them again, later in the episode — different ambush]
jokes.setup: Ross continues his campaign to ambush Monica and Rachel to prove their lack of unagi.
jokes.punchline: Another jump-scare 'Danger!' — the running gag has evolved into Ross just creeping around looking for opportunities.
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the attack gag. Still gets a laugh from the running gag momentum but diminishing returns are setting in without an escalating twist. The setup here is the same as before.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You can't hurt me, Ross. I'm not even really here. I'm a spirit, remember? I died in childbirth in 1881.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? No, you didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, not in THIS lifetime.

jokes.text: 2000 bucks is a lot of money. I wish I had a twin. Where could I find someone who looks exactly like me?
jokes.setup: Joey learns he could earn $2000 in a twin study if only he had an identical twin.
jokes.punchline: He muses aloud 'Where could I find someone who looks exactly like me?' — the answer being obvious (another actor, a lookalike) but Joey acts as if this is a profound unsolvable puzzle.
jokes.explanation: Joey treating a problem that has an obvious solution (hire a lookalike actor) as though it's cosmically mysterious is good character work. The setup is good for what follows (the Carl subplot) but as a standalone beat it's moderate.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're telling me there's money in this?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How much are we talking here?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, sign me up! I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, oh, oh! But wait—do you need my identical twin for this study or something?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because I think I know a guy. Actually, no, I don't think that's gonna work out.

jokes.text: Chandler. / I sensed it was you.
jokes.setup: Chandler comes to find Ross. Ross greets him before he announces himself.
jokes.punchline: 'I sensed it was you' — Ross trying to claim his 'unagi' powers extended to sensing Chandler's arrival, playing the mystic card.
jokes.explanation: Ross extending 'unagi' to ordinary social situations is consistent and funny. The delivery of 'I sensed it was you' as though it's a demonstration of mystical awareness — when it's obviously just recognizing a friend — is a solid beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I knew you were coming.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm psychic.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're psychic? You didn't know Monica was dating Chandler until we told you!

jokes.text: Are you aware that unagi is an eel?
jokes.setup: Ross is performing his 'unagi' mysticism for Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, clearly already informed about the sushi situation, deflates Ross with the same correction Monica and Rachel used.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the eel correction works as a running gag — by now the audience anticipates the eel correction and enjoys the repetition. Chandler's flat delivery makes it land crisply.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not just a soup, it's a way of life. Unagi gives you a kind of sixth sense.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, or it could be the high sodium content.

jokes.text: Why don't you make her one of your little jokes?
jokes.setup: Chandler is panicking about what to make Monica for Valentine's Day.
jokes.punchline: Ross suggests Chandler make her 'one of your little jokes' — a withering dismissal of Chandler's sense of humor as a craft item, not a gift.
jokes.explanation: Ross subtly mocking Chandler's humor as not a real skill ('little jokes') is good friend-group comedy. The condescension is affectionate but pointed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey Chandler, I made something that might help you feel better.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Aw, that's really sweet, man. What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a volcano. I made it in the fourth grade.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A volcano? How is a volcano going to help me?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, when you're feeling down, you just add the baking soda and vinegar, and it erupts. It's very therapeutic.

jokes.text: I could use that. I could say, 'Your love sends me to the moon.' / Except Apollo 8 didn't actually land on the moon. / You can say, 'Your love lets me orbit the moon twice and return safely.'
jokes.setup: Ross offers his sixth-grade Apollo 8 model as a romantic gift Chandler could claim. Chandler tries to make it romantic.
jokes.punchline: Ross's pedantic correction that Apollo 8 only orbited (didn't land), followed by offering the corrected but completely unromantic alternative quote.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the whole run. The structure is perfect: Chandler's romantic attempt, Ross's factual correction, then Ross offering the pedantically accurate but tonally catastrophic alternative ('orbit the moon twice and return safely'). It's a pure distillation of Ross's character — he genuinely thinks the corrected version is acceptable. Only Ross Geller would destroy a romantic gesture with aerospace facts and then be baffled why it doesn't work. Comfortably earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh wow, look at this! You know what this says to me? It says, 'I'm alone.'

jokes.text: I can't give this to her. / Why not? / It says 'Captain Ross' on the side. / And it says 'I hate Monica' on the bottom.
jokes.setup: Chandler considers using Ross's childhood Apollo 8 model as his Valentine's gift.
jokes.punchline: Two disqualifying details emerge: 'Captain Ross' on the side, then — worse — 'I hate Monica' on the bottom, implying Ross's childhood feelings about his sister.
jokes.explanation: Classic double-punchline structure. First disqualifier ('Captain Ross') is funny; second ('I hate Monica') is a revelation that escalates beautifully. The childhood sibling rivalry preserved in handwriting on a craft project is a perfect character-history joke. The beat between the two lines is essential — 'and it says 'I hate Monica' on the bottom' landing after a pause earns the bigger laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm like an astronaut, landing on the moon of your heart.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, the moon's surface is composed of regolith, and the lunar module's descent engine produces approximately 10,500 pounds of thrust. Also, the moon has no atmosphere, so 'landing' would involve a controlled descent using the reaction control system thrusters.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? The moment's gone.

jokes.text: Danger! [Another Ross ambush — this time at the apartment door, later in the episode]
jokes.setup: Continuation of Ross's unagi ambush campaign.
jokes.punchline: Yet another jump-out attack — by now the gag is fully established as a bit.
jokes.explanation: By this third-or-fourth iteration (depending on count), the gag is on autopilot. It still gets a reaction from running gag momentum, but it's the weakest of the Danger! beats in isolation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more interested in space facts?

jokes.text: Salmon-skin roll. [Monica and Rachel walk past Ross's hiding spot holding sushi]
jokes.setup: Earlier Rachel said 'I would kill for a salmon-skin roll right now' in the middle of Ross's unagi lecture.
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts to them actually having gotten sushi — and the visual of the sushi box as they walk past Ross (who is presumably still lecturing/attacking) is the callback payoff.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words ('salmon-skin roll') and a visual do all the work. The callback to Rachel's food distraction now pays off visually. They literally went and got the sushi instead of engaging with Ross's unagi lecture further. It's also a subtle character comment on their priorities. One of the most economical jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't give it to Monica because it says 'World's Best Big Brother' on it.

jokes.text: Yes, honey, I made it myself. [Monica on the phone, clearly buying a gift rather than making it]
jokes.setup: Monica promised to make Chandler's Valentine's gift but has been unable to.
jokes.punchline: She's apparently on the phone with a store, saying 'Yes, honey, I made it myself' — practicing her lie or telling the store clerk the cover story she'll use with Chandler.
jokes.explanation: The irony of Monica — a professional chef, famously overachieving — having to fake a homemade gift is very funny. The overheard phone snippet works because we only get one side and have to piece it together.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Even worse, the inscription says 'To Monica, the only woman who could ever satisfy me.' Now it just looks like I'm bragging about my wife's... abilities.

jokes.text: A mixed tape! A mixed tape! [Chandler has a eureka moment]
jokes.setup: Chandler has been desperately trying to figure out what to make Monica for Valentine's Day.
jokes.punchline: His breakthrough — a mixed tape — is delivered with the triumphant energy of someone who has solved a major problem, while the audience recognizes this as a relatively simple and not particularly special gift.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's disproportionate excitement over a mixed tape is relatable and character-consistent — he's been failing at crafts and grasps the first achievable option with both hands. The double-shout 'A mixed tape! A mixed tape!' reads as comedically over-the-top.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's unagi. The eel. It's a real thing. I'm prepared.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You never know when you're going to be attacked, so I'm teaching you unagi—the art of sensing danger.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, he's finally lost it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You scoff, but unagi has saved my life more times than I can count. Zero. But it could happen!

jokes.text: It's a sock bunny. / Remember how I call you bunny? / Not really. / I did one time. And I want to start doing it more.
jokes.setup: Chandler presents Monica's gift — Phoebe's sock bunny, which he's trying to pass off as his own creation.
jokes.punchline: The invented nickname 'bunny' — Monica doesn't remember it because Chandler made it up on the spot to justify the gift — and Chandler's immediate backfill ('I did one time. And I want to start doing it more') is painfully transparent.
jokes.explanation: Monica's flat 'Not really' is perfect — she's not angry, just factual, which makes Chandler's escalating lie ('I did one time. And I want to start doing it more.') funnier. The whole sequence is about Chandler digging himself deeper with a lie he immediately has to prop up.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I'll have the unagi.

jokes.text: Phoebe makes sock bunnies. / No, she doesn't. What she makes, they're sock rabbits. They're completely different.
jokes.setup: Monica has figured out Chandler's sock bunny came from Phoebe, not from him.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's desperate distinction between 'sock bunnies' (Phoebe's) and 'sock rabbits' (his) — a distinction that obviously doesn't exist — is a pure panic move.
jokes.explanation: The 'bunny vs. rabbit' distinction is an inspired piece of Chandler-panic writing. The more specific the lie, the more obviously false it is. 'They're completely different' said with any confidence at all is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I didn't get you anything.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because... I forgot.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You forgot?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I totally forgot. It completely slipped my mind.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? I'm serious! I would never lie to you. I'm telling you the absolute truth right now.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Then why is there a gift-wrapped box behind your back?

jokes.text: I didn't make it! I forgot about tonight and that we're supposed to make the presents.
jokes.setup: Chandler's sock bunny/rabbit distinction has completely failed.
jokes.punchline: He immediately capitulates and confesses — but then the irony lands: Monica also didn't make her gift, which we learn shortly after.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the symmetric reveal that Monica also failed. Chandler's admission is straightforward but it sets up the irony coming in the next beats.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh God, oh God, what am I gonna get her? I have no idea what to get her!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, just get her a gift certificate.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A gift certificate? That's so impersonal!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, it's not impersonal if you write a nice card.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A gift certificate AND a card? Why didn't I think of that? I'm a genius!

jokes.text: I am going to cook you anything you want in here. / And I'm going to do anything you want in there.
jokes.setup: Chandler is apologizing for forgetting Monica's gift and offering to make it up to her.
jokes.punchline: 'Anything you want in here' (kitchen) + 'anything you want in there' (bedroom) — the architecture of the apartment does the work. The pause between the two clauses is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom innuendo construction — the euphemism works because 'in here/in there' is clean but pointed. The delivery beat between kitchen and bedroom is essential and the audience would reward it. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I got you a sock bunny. I know I never called you that, but... it's adorable, it's soft, and occasionally it goes missing for no reason.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not a pet name, that's a cry for help.

jokes.text: Well, I did put a lot of thought into the tape.
jokes.setup: Chandler has offered cooking AND bedroom service in exchange for forgiveness. Monica is considering.
jokes.punchline: Monica's response — 'Well, I did put a lot of thought into the tape' — is a fake-humility acceptance that also hints she plans to milk this for all it's worth.
jokes.explanation: Monica accepting Chandler's apology offer while playing up her sacrifice is perfectly Monica — she's simultaneously forgiving him AND extracting maximum value from the situation. The ironic modesty of 'a lot of thought' for a mix tape (not exactly a Sistine Chapel) is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, this is amazing! Did you really make this?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I did it myself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, there's a difference between making something and making something yourself.

jokes.text: You are way too young to have seen that.
jokes.setup: An unspecified sexual act has been implied by 'anything you want in there' — Chandler and Monica are apparently doing something.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's comment 'You are way too young to have seen that' is addressed to someone who walked in on them — implying a visual comedy moment the audience doesn't fully see but can infer.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in what it implies without showing. 'Way too young to have seen that' works as a PG-rated indicator of something R-rated happening — the audience fills in the blank. Good innuendo construction.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I can't do this anymore. I have to tell you something.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There is no sock bunny. I made it up. I created an entire fictional rabbit out of hosiery and lies, and I've been living with that guilt every single day.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.

jokes.text: Your birthday's in a month and a half. What if I forget to get you a present for that too? / You are totally and completely 100 percent forgiven.
jokes.setup: Monica has just forgiven Chandler for forgetting the Valentine's gift.
jokes.punchline: Chandler pre-emptively reminds Monica about his likely forgetting her birthday — Monica instantly offers full forgiveness for THAT too, before it even happens.
jokes.explanation: Smart character moment — Chandler's pre-emptive apology (essentially banking forgiveness) and Monica immediately agreeing because she's already getting cooking + bedroom privileges. It's both a character joke about their relationship dynamics AND a solid construction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's okay, Chandler. I love it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? Because I didn't wrap it or anything.

jokes.text: It's like that old saying, 'Have sex, eat some cake.'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are celebrating reconciliation. Monica's cake is ready.
jokes.punchline: Chandler invents a fake 'old saying' that describes exactly and only what they are literally doing — the joke being that it's not an old saying at all.
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed. The 'old saying' framing implies wisdom/antiquity, but the saying is both completely literal and completely specific to this moment. 'Have sex, eat some cake' is funny partly because it's the exact correct description of what they're doing, treated as proverbial wisdom. A very Chandler joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What do you want to do tonight?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, there's an old saying: 'A friend in need is a friend who owes you money.'

jokes.text: Hey, Mon. Hey, Chan. Just getting a soda. [Joey walks in on Chandler and Monica]
jokes.setup: Chandler has just delivered a funny line about 'have sex, eat some cake' — implying they just had sex.
jokes.punchline: Joey wanders in completely obliviously and helps himself to a soda, treating their clearly post-intimate scenario as totally normal.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom interruption gag — the friend who walks in on the wrong moment and is oblivious. Joey's 'just getting a soda' is functionally funny but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Who the hell are you? / I'm Joey. / How are you doing?
jokes.setup: Monica is startled to see what appears to be a stranger, who she doesn't recognize as Joey.
jokes.punchline: The stranger introduces himself as 'Joey' — and then delivers Joey's signature 'How are you doing?' pickup line, confirming this is Carl, the hired Joey lookalike, completely in character.
jokes.explanation: The reveal works because 'How are you doing?' is so recognizably Joey's catchphrase that having a stranger deploy it is immediately jarring and funny. The audience understands before Monica does, which creates a nice brief dramatic irony.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No no no, you gotta say it like this: 'How you doin'?'

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: How you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, with more... charm. More... Joey. 'How you doin'?'

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: How you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, forget it. Just... just stand there and look handsome.

jokes.text: No! No! No! No! / How you doing? How you doing? Damn it, Carl! Go wait in the hall.
jokes.setup: Carl (Joey's hired lookalike) is hitting on Monica using Joey's catchphrase.
jokes.punchline: Joey rushes in to control Carl, but Carl keeps repeating the catchphrase even as Joey is yelling at him — Carl is committed to being Joey to a fault.
jokes.explanation: Carl's inability to stop doing the bit even while being told to stop is very funny — he's such a bad actor that he can't break character even in a crisis. 'Damn it, Carl!' is a great exasperated punchline. The repeated 'How you doing?' as Joey desperately tries to shut him down escalates nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I hired my twin brother Carl to be my stand-in for auditions.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, you have a twin brother?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, and he's a great actor. Well, actually he's not, but he looks exactly like me, so...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not how this works.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not? I show up, they see me, then Carl shows up, they see me again. They're gonna think I'm amazing!

jokes.text: Sometimes the good ideas are right in front of you.
jokes.setup: Joey has just explained that he hired another actor to pretend to be his twin to get $2000 from a research study.
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers this as wisdom — 'sometimes the good ideas are right in front of you' — presenting an elaborate scam as obvious common sense.
jokes.explanation: Joey's self-congratulatory tone about an idea that is objectively deceptive and probably illegal is funny. The aphorism framing elevates it slightly above a basic character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Carl, this guy's a total mess. He can't act. Watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh no, my cat is stuck in a tree.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh no! My cat is stuck in a tree!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: OH NO! MY CAT IS STUCK IN A TREE! OH MY GOD!

jokes.text: It sounds crazy, but it might work. The only problem is Carl's acting... / The only problem?
jokes.setup: Joey explains his plan to use Carl as a fake twin for the medical study.
jokes.punchline: Joey identifies Carl's bad acting as 'the only problem' — Monica's incredulous 'The only problem?' calls out that there are MANY obvious problems with this plan (impersonation, fraud, etc.).
jokes.explanation: Monica as the voice of reason calling out Joey's tunnel vision is a solid comedic beat. The 'only problem?' is a well-worn structure but executed cleanly here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I could take any game show host. I'm serious! I could beat up Bob Barker, Alex Trebek, any of them.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Even Regis?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Especially Regis!

jokes.text: He's the reason I didn't get that big commercial a couple of years ago. We were supposed to be brothers, but he messed up.
jokes.setup: Joey is explaining Carl's acting problem.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Joey has worked with Carl before — and Carl ruined a previous job — makes the choice to hire him again obviously stupid, which is very Joey.
jokes.explanation: The fact that Joey chose the one actor he KNOWS has caused him problems is perfect Joey logic. Good character-specific comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not 'I am unagi.' The plural of unagi is unagi.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So we're supposed to say 'we are unagi'?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No! You don't understand. Unagi is a state of total awareness.

jokes.text: Can I get a piece of that cake? / Pizza! We like pizza! Get out!
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to manage Carl's behavior and explain him to Monica.
jokes.punchline: Carl asks for cake — breaking from Joey's instructions — and Joey's frantic correction ('Pizza! We like pizza!') while simultaneously shooing him out reveals Joey desperately trying to maintain the twin fiction while Carl freelances.
jokes.explanation: 'Pizza! We like pizza! Get out!' is excellent. Joey improvising that he and his 'twin' share a pizza preference while ejecting Carl is chaotic and very funny. The overlap of maintaining the lie AND getting rid of Carl is a lot of comedy crammed into a few words.

jokes.text: Pat Sajak? / Yep. / Alex Trebek? / Of course. / Chuck Woolery? / Definitely. / You will not find a single game-show host whose ass I cannot kick.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to prove his martial arts prowess. The women are quizzing him on specific opponents.
jokes.punchline: Ross confidently claims he could beat up any game-show host — a highly specific, oddly non-threatening category of people to specialize in fighting.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The list structure (Sajak, Trebek, Woolery — escalating specificity of game show hosts) followed by Ross's total confidence in this extremely niche fighting specialty is brilliant. It's unexpected, specific, and perfectly absurd. The escalation through three hosts before the punchline is textbook joke structure. Easily an 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, Carl, remember what I told you. Don't talk. Just stand there and look good.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got it. No talking. I can do that.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Carl...

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: Right, right, sorry. I'm done. Lips are sealed.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: So anyway, about my agent...

jokes.text: Say it! Say we are unagi! / It's not something you are, it's something you have.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel have apparently gotten the upper hand on Ross physically and are demanding he say they have 'unagi.'
jokes.punchline: Even while being physically dominated, Ross corrects their grammar/usage of 'unagi' — 'it's not something you ARE, it's something you HAVE' — his pedantry overriding his physical defeat.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Ross being physically pinned and still finding the grammatical error more urgent to correct than his defeat is a perfect crystallization of his character. 'It's not something you ARE, it's something you HAVE' is the most Ross Geller sentence ever written. Very high character integration justified.

dialogue.speaker: Researcher
dialogue.line: You guys aren't twins.

jokes.text: I could easily get out of this... but there's a chance you could get very, very hurt!
jokes.setup: Ross is being physically pinned by Monica and Rachel after his grammar correction failed to free him.
jokes.punchline: Ross claims he could escape but won't for THEIR safety — a face-saving rationalization that is transparently false.
jokes.explanation: Ross would absolutely say exactly this. The logic inversion — 'I'm not escaping to protect YOU' — is a perfect piece of defensive face-saving that only an ego like Ross's could produce. The concern in his voice for their safety while he's being pinned is what sells it. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is all Carl's fault!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How was I supposed to know he'd show up looking nothing like me?

jokes.text: Carl, we're next. Now remember, what is this not gonna be? / Another Minute Maid fiasco. / That's right. And what are you not gonna do? / I'm not gonna talk because.. / Damn it, Carl!
jokes.setup: Joey is prepping Carl before they enter the research facility, drilling him on what NOT to do.
jokes.punchline: Carl correctly starts the answer 'I'm not gonna talk because...' — and then, in answering, begins to talk, which IS the thing he's not supposed to do. 'Damn it, Carl!' is Joey's exasperated response.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic construction. The joke is a logical trap: Joey asks Carl to explain why he won't talk — which requires talking. Carl falls into the trap immediately by beginning to explain, thus doing the thing he's not supposed to do, mid-explanation about not doing it. 'Damn it, Carl!' is perfectly timed. This is the most structurally sophisticated joke in the episode and among the funniest. Clear 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I made us a five-course meal.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? What are we having?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Cereal, a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, chocolate milk, cookies, and ice cream. I paired each course with a different blanket from the couch.

jokes.text: Joey and Tony Tribbiani. / That's us. / But this is a study for identical twins. / That's right. $2000.
jokes.setup: Joey and Carl present themselves as twins named 'Joey and Tony Tribbiani'
jokes.punchline: When told it's a twin study, Joey responds 'That's right. $2000.' — confirming he understands the requirements only in terms of the payment
jokes.explanation: Joey's '$2000' response to being told they need to be identical twins is funny in its irrelevance — he treats the payment as the confirmation of success rather than their physical appearance. Good character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is nice.

jokes.text: But you're not identical twins. / Damn it, Carl!
jokes.setup: Joey and Carl present themselves as identical twins 'Joey and Tony Tribbiani' to get into the study.
jokes.punchline: The researcher immediately sees through the deception — they're obviously not identical. Joey's response is 'Damn it, Carl!' — blaming Carl for their obvious physical mismatch, as though Carl somehow caused this.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Carl subplot. 'Damn it, Carl!' has been building as a running exasperation, and using it here — when the problem is literally that they look nothing alike, something that is NOT Carl's fault — is the ideal payoff. Joey reflexively blaming Carl for an unfixable situation is both character-perfect and structurally satisfying. The economy of two words to end the entire subplot is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I made you a mixtape.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my god, that's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God.

jokes.text: Continuing the countdown of your favorite meals. Tonight, number three: Macaroni and cheese with cut-up hot dogs.
jokes.setup: Chandler promised to cook Monica anything she wanted. This scene reveals what that has meant.
jokes.punchline: Chandler has apparently been doing a countdown of Monica's (or his own) favorite meals — and number three is 'macaroni and cheese with cut-up hot dogs,' a profound contrast with Monica's professional chef status.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the gap between what 'cooking anything you want' implies (gourmet, effort) and what Chandler actually delivers (mac and cheese with hot dogs). The 'countdown' framing — presenting pedestrian meals with Food Network gravitas — is a nice structural touch.

dialogue.speaker: Self-defense instructor
dialogue.line: Well, that was terrible. But you know what? This is actually a great learning opportunity for you.

dialogue.speaker: Self-defense instructor
dialogue.line: You see, the key thing you did wrong was... basically everything.

dialogue.speaker: Self-defense instructor
dialogue.line: But the important lesson here is: next time, try to keep your hands up.

jokes.text: 'The Way You Look Tonight' is on here. Dance with me.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are dancing to the mixed tape; Chandler earlier promised this song would be on it
jokes.punchline: The sweet romantic moment is entirely built on a lie — this is Janice's tape and Chandler had no idea what was on it
jokes.explanation: Dramatic irony beat — the audience is primed to know this is Janice's tape. 'The Way You Look Tonight' being on it both validates Chandler's claim (accidentally true) and deepens the comedic trap. The reveal is coming.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not very good at it. I got beat up by a girl.

jokes.text: That's why I made you this tape. Happy birthday! Love, Janice!
jokes.setup: Monica has been letting Chandler believe the romantic mixed tape was made just for him. 'The Way You Look Tonight' plays. The moment is romantic and sweet.
jokes.punchline: Janice's voice comes on the tape — it was originally Janice's gift to Chandler from a previous relationship — with 'Happy birthday! Love, Janice!'
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. It works on multiple levels: (1) Monica is caught not having made the tape herself — she's been lying just like Chandler; (2) The tape is from JANICE, Chandler's most famous and dreaded ex-girlfriend, whose voice is an instant laugh trigger; (3) the contrast between the romantic moment ('The Way You Look Tonight') and 'Happy birthday! Love, Janice!' is a maximally jarring deflation; (4) it reveals that Chandler has been re-gifting a Janice tape — which raises many uncomfortable questions. Perfect structure, perfect timing, perfect character payoff. Easily the standout moment of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.line: You tried to attack your ex-wife?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I tried. She got away.

jokes.text: No, you're the sweetest.
jokes.setup: Monica has just been caught out using Janice's old tape as her handmade gift. The situation is mutually embarrassing — both failed.
jokes.punchline: Chandler responds 'No, you're the sweetest' — a bizarrely gracious and entirely ironic response to being exposed as a re-gifter of his ex's tape.
jokes.explanation: The button on the Janice tape reveal. 'No, you're the sweetest' — in full ironic awareness that neither of them followed through on the promise — is a perfect close to their storyline. The mutual embarrassment allowing them to mutually forgive is sweet AND funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I need to learn self-defense. Can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: Self-defense instructor
dialogue.line: Sure, I can teach you. Tell you what - we should team up and attack women.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Self-defense instructor
dialogue.line: It's the best way to learn - you need real-world practice with actual victims.

jokes.text: I tried attacking two women. Did not work. / What? / No, it's okay. They're my friends. In fact, I was married to one of them.
jokes.setup: Ross explains to the self-defense instructor why he's seeking advice on attacking people.
jokes.punchline: Ross's clarification — 'it's okay, they're my friends, I was married to one of them' — doesn't make the situation better at all. Attacking your friends/ex-wife is not less alarming than attacking strangers.
jokes.explanation: Ross genuinely thinking 'they're my friends, I was married to one of them' is a reassuring detail — when it makes everything much worse — is perfect obtuse character comedy. The self-defense instructor's perspective makes the already-absurd unagi storyline land fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.line: Let's attack women together.

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.line: Wait, that came out wrong.

jokes.text: No, it's okay. They're my friends. In fact, I was married to one of them.
jokes.setup: The instructor is alarmed that Ross attacked two women
jokes.punchline: Ross reassures her with 'In fact, I was married to one of them' — which does not reassure at all, implying attacking an ex-wife is fine
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark subversive joke. 'In fact, I was married to one of them' is offered as REASSURANCE — as if that makes it better — and of course it makes it considerably worse. Ross's complete lack of awareness that this is alarming is entirely character-consistent. Great economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, uh, how's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? I'm just... talking to some people.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Dude, you're literally crouching behind the counter.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not crouching, I'm... examining the pastries at eye level.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you're doing that thing again.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What thing?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: The creepy stalker thing. You look like a supervillain planning world domination.

jokes.text: You attacked your ex-wife? / Oh, no. No, no. / I tried. / But I couldn't. That's why I'm here.
jokes.setup: Ross has said he was married to one of the women he tried to attack
jokes.punchline: He corrects the instructor — he didn't succeed in attacking his ex-wife, he TRIED and FAILED, which is why he's here for lessons — presented as a relatively positive clarification
jokes.explanation: Exceptional escalation. Ross's clarification — 'Oh, no. No, no. I tried. But I couldn't. That's why I'm here.' — reframes failed attacks on women as a deficiency to be corrected, not a moral issue. The deadpan structure is perfect: denial, then admission of attempt, then the kicker 'That's why I'm here.' He's seeking professional instruction to better attack women. The instructor's horror is the unstated punchline. This rivals the best jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not attacking women, I'm attacking you!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we're losing to girls!

jokes.text: Maybe we could attack them together!
jokes.setup: Ross explains he tried to attack two women (his friends) and failed. He's seeking the instructor's help.
jokes.punchline: The instructor enthusiastically suggests they team up to attack Ross's friends together — completely crossing professional and ethical lines with cheerful obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: The self-defense instructor being so enthusiastic about ambushing random women that they volunteer to join is a great absurdist escalation. The cheerful 'Maybe we could attack them together!' from someone in a position of authority is brilliantly wrong.

jokes.text: That's a no.
jokes.setup: The self-defense instructor has just suggested teaming up to attack Monica and Rachel.
jokes.punchline: Ross's flat 'That's a no' — the most understated response to an objectively insane proposal.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum economy. 'That's a no' is Ross at his most deadpan, shutting down an absurd suggestion with the calmness of someone who is entirely familiar with absurd suggestions. The economy score is a perfect 10 — you cannot say less and convey more.

jokes.text: And I will cook anything you want in here... and do anything you want in there. / Yeah, you will!
jokes.setup: Chandler is again apologizing to Monica for the Janice tape situation.
jokes.punchline: He repeats his earlier 'in here / in there' offer — but this time Monica's enthusiastic 'Yeah, you will!' shows she's not letting him off easy and is fully expecting delivery.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the earlier offer — this time with Monica's confident 'Yeah, you will!' adding a new dimension. Diminished returns on the structure itself, but Monica's delivery makes it land.

jokes.text: And I will cook anything you want in here... and do anything you want in there. / Yeah, you will! And are you kidding me?
jokes.setup: Ross is apologizing profusely to the instructor for the whole exchange
jokes.punchline: He offers to cook for her and 'do anything in there' — accidentally using the same apologetic formula he presumably overheard from Chandler earlier; the instructor's enthusiastic 'Yeah, you will!' suggests she is very open to both offers
jokes.explanation: Callback to Chandler's formula with Ross now deploying it to get out of his own mess. The instructor's enthusiastic acceptance is the unexpected punchline — she's attracted to this strange man who tried to attack women and is now offering domestic and sexual services. Solid but not among the episode's best.

jokes.text: Come on, Monica, it's our Valentine's Day. Please, please, please, please?
jokes.setup: Chandler is begging Monica for something (sex, apparently) on Valentine's Day after the Janice tape disaster
jokes.punchline: His repeated 'please, please, please, please?' mirrors Joey's earlier begging technique — and the callback to 'it helps if you've got a little of this going on' (the begging face) is implied
jokes.explanation: Functional character moment — Chandler's desperation is in-character — but the joke is thin. It's situation comedy rather than a crafted joke. The repeated 'please' is performance-dependent.

jokes.text: Nowhere to run.
jokes.setup: Ross has apparently cornered Monica and Rachel again for another unagi ambush.
jokes.punchline: 'Nowhere to run' — delivered with Ross's signature unhinged confidence about a situation that is objectively him stalking his friends.
jokes.explanation: Three words delivered with villain confidence by a paleontologist lecturing his friends about eel-based martial philosophy. The gap between what Ross thinks is happening (demonstrating superior awareness) and what is actually happening (harassment) is the sustained joke of the unagi subplot.

jokes.text: Nowhere to run. [Ross confronts Rachel and Phoebe, presumably having collaborated with the self-defense instructor for a final showdown]
jokes.setup: Ross has apparently set a trap for Rachel and Phoebe
jokes.punchline: 'Nowhere to run' as villain-movie dialogue — Ross is now playing an action-movie antagonist in his self-defense war
jokes.explanation: Ross's adoption of action-movie language ('Nowhere to run') is funny in its escalation — he's fully committed to the bit at this point. Visual gag territory for the climactic confrontation.

jokes.text: Why is Ross doing that? / Danger! / Oh, my God! Why is he jumping on those women?
jokes.setup: Ross has apparently escalated to jumping on two strangers he mistook for Monica and Rachel.
jokes.punchline: A bystander narrates what Ross is doing — 'Why is he jumping on those women?' — from an outside perspective that makes the full insanity of the unagi subplot visible.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing escalation. The unagi subplot has built from an abstract lecture to actual physical attacks, and the climax — Ross jumping on two STRANGERS who he thought were Monica and Rachel — is shown through the eyes of horrified bystanders. 'Why is he jumping on those women?' is the ideal punchline to end the entire A-story on. The outsider perspective reframes everything the audience has normalized as objectively deranged.

jokes.text: We should help them. / I don't think they need any help.
jokes.setup: Ross is attacking two strangers. Monica and Rachel watch.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'I don't think they need any help' — implying the two strangers are handily defeating Ross — is the final button on the unagi storyline. His victims turned out to be better fighters than him.
jokes.explanation: Perfect closing line for the episode's A-plot. 'I don't think they need any help' closes the loop — the women Ross thought lacked unagi are watching Ross get beaten up by strangers, while they don't even bother intervening. The self-defense class subplot pays off here as well: the women who Ross said couldn't fight are now passive observers of his defeat. Structurally complete.

tmdb_overview: At the end of semester Ross gets his student evaluations and one of them writes that he's hot. It turns out to be a cute girl named Elizabeth and even though it could cost him his job, Ross considers dating her. An ex-girlfriend of Chandler's from college is directing the new Al Pacino movie and Joey asks Chandler for help with getting an audition. Meanwhile, after a fire ruins Phoebe and Rachel's apartment, they're forced to find temporary living spaces with Monica and Joey.
insight: Ross's student romance scandal generates 76 jokes but lands softly at 73.9 without a single standout punchline.
